newsitem.title: GERMANY: Fischler puts farm price tag on EU expansion east.
newsitem.headline: Fischler puts farm price tag on EU expansion east.

text.p: The costs of handling agricultural surpluses from the European Union's inclusion of 10 eastern European countries (CEECs) may total 12 billion Ecus a year, EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said on Saturday.
Speaking at an East-West forum held at Berlin's Green Week agricultural fair, he said these annual costs would arise in the first decade of the next millennium, if the ten joined.
"This would represent about 30 percent of today's total spending on agricultural support in the EU," he said.
The surpluses would also be problematic because there would be limits on their exportability with the help of subsidies.
This meant the EU needed to step up its farm reform efforts, but not just to include the East.

Even without integrating new members, the EU was set to produce surpluses in beef, grain, milk, olive oil and wine and it needed to move beyond its traditional volume-cutting measures to handle them, Fischler said.
He stressed that he did not want a radical change of the common agricultural policy (CAP), nor did he wish to abandon it.

But faced with the CEECs arrival, new internal financial contraints and pressure to comply with new liberalisation and market access rules expected from the next round of trade talks in 1999, the EU needed to be proactive.
The EU Commission is due to present reports on the applications of the 10 CEECs in the summer of 1997 and accession talks may in theory start in 1998.
Fischler said it was unlikely any new EU members would be admitted before the year 2003.
Bilateral accession talks needed to look at each country's special situation and they should not just focus on farming.
Most eastern farm industries were starved of capital and had grave structural deficits, but in some cases, Brussels might be able to amend earlier, overly pessimistic, studies.
German farm minister Jochen Borchert differed.

The current CAP offered a sound basis, from which to extend membership to the CEECs in a step-by-step approach and with long transition periods as those required in the past from aspiring southern European countries, he said.
Russia's farm minister Viktor Khklystun also addressed the 400-strong audience.
He said through interpreter that Russia, as a part of its ongoing economic restructuring, was helping farmers to get credit and market access, and it welcomed foreign investments.
